stories.headline: AI that studies handwriting suggests many Dead Sea Scrolls are older than thought
stories.what_happened: A team led from the University of Groningen in the Netherlands trained an AI called Enoch on the handwriting of 24 Dead Sea Scroll samples whose age had been measured by radiocarbon dating. They then used it to estimate the age of 135 scrolls that had never been dated. Many came out older than scholars had estimated from the handwriting by eye, and the study was published in PLOS One.
stories.why_its_good: Only 24 samples had a measured radiocarbon age to learn from. The AI used them to give an age estimate for 135 more scrolls from their handwriting alone.
careful: The model learned from only 24 dated samples and its typical error is about 28 to 31 years.
Handwriting experts judged about 79% of its estimates realistic, not all of them.
Press coverage reported that some scroll scholars are not convinced by the earlier dates, so say 'suggests', not 'proves'.
Do not say the Bible has been re-dated.

stories.headline: AI finds that one face in a Raphael painting was probably painted by someone else
stories.what_happened: Researchers from the universities of Bradford, Nottingham and Stanford trained an AI on authenticated paintings by Raphael and pointed it at the Madonna della Rosa, which hangs in the Prado in Madrid. Tested as a whole, the painting gave no clear answer. Tested piece by piece, most of it came out as Raphael's work, but the face of Joseph most likely did not. The study was published in the journal Heritage Science.
stories.why_its_good: The AI gave art experts a new kind of evidence about who painted what, and it pointed to one specific face in a famous picture.
careful: The researchers say the result is not enough on its own to decide who painted what. It is one tool to help experts.
The 98% accuracy figure is the team's own test result for the model.
Giulio Romano is only suggested as a possible painter of Joseph's face.
Some art historians were dismissive of the work in press coverage, and the Prado has not changed its attribution as far as we found.
The journal page could not be opened directly: facts were confirmed on the University of Nottingham's own news page.

stories.headline: AI repaints the edges of Rembrandt's Night Watch that were cut off 300 years ago
stories.what_happened: In 1715 Rembrandt's Night Watch was trimmed on all four sides to fit a wall in Amsterdam's City Hall, and the strips were never found. In June 2021 the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam showed the painting complete for the first time in 300 years. Its scientists had taught an AI Rembrandt's technique and colours, then had it recreate the missing parts from a small copy made in the 17th century. The new pieces were printed and hung around the original.
stories.why_its_good: The AI turned another painter's small copy into Rembrandt's own style at full size, so visitors saw the picture as he composed it, including 64 centimetres on the left that had been lost.
careful: The added pieces are printed reconstructions placed around the painting, not recovered Rembrandt paint.
The display was temporary, for some months in 2021, and the museum said it would not add the pieces in the real restoration.
The reconstruction rests on a 17th-century copy attributed to Gerrit Lundens.

stories.headline: AI spots an unknown play by Lope de Vega among anonymous manuscripts in Spain's National Library
stories.what_happened: Researchers from the universities of Valladolid and Vienna used AI to transcribe about 1,300 plays from Spain's Golden Age, then compared the wording of each with known authors. One anonymous manuscript in the National Library of Spain, La francesa Laura, matched Lope de Vega, one of Spain's greatest playwrights. The researchers then checked it by traditional methods, including its verse, and the library announced the find in early 2023.
stories.why_its_good: The play had sat in the library's catalogue since 1882 with no author. AI read the handwriting in hours and picked it out from the pile, which let scholars focus their checking on the right manuscript.
careful: The attribution rests on writing style, checked by scholars. No document names Lope as the author.
Say 'attributed to', and that the play dates from the last years before his death in 1635.
The National Library's own announcement could not be opened: facts were confirmed on University of Valladolid and University of Innsbruck pages and in news reports.

stories.headline: Machine learning backs the old theory that Shakespeare shared the writing of Henry VIII
stories.what_happened: Petr Plecháč of the Czech Academy of Sciences trained a machine learning model on the favourite words and verse rhythms of Shakespeare and of a second playwright named Fletcher. He ran it across the play Henry VIII passage by passage, ignoring scene breaks. The result strongly supported the split between the two writers that a scholar named James Spedding had proposed long before, and the study was published in Digital Scholarship in the Humanities.
stories.why_its_good: Scholars had argued over who wrote which parts of the play using their own ear for style. The AI measured word habits and rhythm across the whole text and came to the same division independently.
careful: It supports an existing theory. It did not discover the collaboration.
The paper's summary does not give a percentage for each writer, so do not say 'half'.
This is statistical evidence about style, not a document proving who wrote what.

stories.headline: AI helps piece together a lost hymn in praise of Babylon
stories.what_happened: Enrique Jiménez of LMU Munich, working with the University of Baghdad, rediscovered a hymn in praise of the ancient city of Babylon, written around 1000 BCE and about 250 lines long. His team is digitising clay tablet fragments from around the world and uses AI to find pieces that belong to the same text. The AI turned up 30 more manuscripts of the hymn, which let the scholars fill in the missing parts. The work was published in the journal Iraq.
stories.why_its_good: Matching scattered fragments by hand would have taken decades, the lead researcher said. With AI the team recovered a poem describing Babylon's buildings, the Euphrates bringing spring to the fields, and the city's priestesses.
careful: 'Would have taken decades' is the researcher's own estimate.
The AI matched fragments. Scholars did the reading and translation.
Facts come from LMU's own news page describing the peer-reviewed paper (DOI 10.1017/irq.2024.23), which was not opened directly.

stories.headline: AI learns to tell a happy pig from an unhappy one by its grunts
stories.what_happened: A team of European researchers, including scientists at the University of Copenhagen and ETH Zurich, recorded 7,414 calls from 411 pigs in situations from birth to slaughter. They trained an AI to tell from the sound alone whether the pig was in a good or bad situation, and it got it right 91.5% of the time. The study was published in Scientific Reports.
stories.why_its_good: A standard statistical method managed only about 62% on the same recordings. The authors say the result shows an automated system for checking pig welfare on farms can be built.
careful: Nothing is in use on farms yet. This is a study on recorded calls.
The AI sorts calls into positive or negative situations as defined by the researchers. It does not read a pig's mind.
Its accuracy at naming the exact situation was lower, at 81.5%.

stories.headline: AI learns to hold and shape the super-hot gas inside a Swiss fusion machine
stories.what_happened: Scientists at EPFL's Swiss Plasma Center in Lausanne and DeepMind trained an AI in a simulator to control the magnets of a fusion machine called TCV. They then let it run the real machine, where it held plasma, a gas heated to hundreds of millions of degrees, in a range of shapes. It also kept two separate plasmas going in the machine at the same time. The results were published in Nature.
stories.why_its_good: One AI system learned to work the magnets for many different plasma shapes. The paper says this reduces the design effort needed each time scientists want a new one.
careful: This is a research machine that makes no electricity. Do not suggest fusion power is close.
DeepMind is a company: the independent sources are the Nature paper and EPFL.

stories.headline: AI trained on 2,000 fossil footprints helps work out which dinosaur made them
stories.what_happened: Researchers led by the Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin, working with the University of Edinburgh, trained an AI on nearly 2,000 fossil footprints. It agreed with human experts about 90% of the time on what kind of dinosaur made a track, including ones experts argue over. It also found that some tracks more than 200 million years old share features with the feet of birds. The study was published in PNAS, and an app called DinoTracker lets anyone upload a photo or sketch of a footprint for analysis.
stories.why_its_good: Fossil footprints are common but hard to read, and experts often disagree. The AI gives a consistent second opinion and puts a tool once limited to specialists in the hands of anyone who finds a track.
careful: The bird-like tracks have two explanations in the source: birds began much earlier than thought, or some early dinosaurs simply had bird-like feet. Do not pick one.
'About 90%' is agreement with experts, who can themselves be wrong.
The source does not say whether the app is free.

stories.headline: AI heart-trace alerts cut deaths among hospital patients in a Taiwan trial
stories.what_happened: Doctors at Tri-Service General Hospital in Taipei ran a trial with 39 physicians and 15,965 patients. An AI read each patient's routine heart trace and sent the doctor a warning when it judged the patient at high risk of dying. Within 90 days, 3.6% of patients whose doctors got the alerts had died, against 4.3% of those whose doctors did not. The trial was published in Nature Medicine.
stories.why_its_good: The AI picked out the patients in most danger from a routine heart trace and warned their doctors. Fewer of those doctors' patients died, in a randomised trial.
careful: One hospital system in Taiwan. It has not yet been repeated elsewhere as far as we found.
The gain was concentrated in patients the AI flagged as high risk.
The authors say exactly how the alerts led to fewer deaths still needs explaining.
Say 3.6% against 4.3%, not 'slashed' or 'halved'.

stories.headline: AI reading routine heart traces helps family doctors catch weak hearts earlier
stories.what_happened: Mayo Clinic ran a trial across 45 clinics and hospitals in Minnesota and Wisconsin with 22,641 adults who were having a routine heart trace. For half of the care teams, an AI read the trace and told the doctor when it saw signs of a weak heart pump. Doctors who got the AI result found more new cases, 2.1% of patients against 1.6%. The trial was published in Nature Medicine.
stories.why_its_good: The AI found a hidden warning in a test patients were already having, so more people with a weak heart were diagnosed, with no significant rise in follow-up heart scans overall.
careful: The rise is from 1.6% to 2.1% of patients: real but modest.
The trial measured new diagnoses, not whether patients lived longer.

stories.headline: With an AI handheld scanner, beginners date pregnancies as well as trained sonographers
stories.what_happened: Researchers from the University of North Carolina and the University of Zambia tested a handheld ultrasound probe with built-in AI on 400 pregnant people in Lusaka, Zambia, and Chapel Hill in the United States. People with no training in ultrasound swept the probe across the belly and the AI estimated how far along the pregnancy was. Their estimates were off by 3.2 days on average, against 3.0 days for trained sonographers. The study was published in JAMA.
stories.why_its_good: The AI did the skilled part of the scan, so someone with no ultrasound training got an answer within a fraction of a day of a trained sonographer's.
careful: This was a study at two sites, not routine use.
The main test covered scans between 14 and 27 weeks of pregnancy.
It estimates how far along a pregnancy is. It does not check the baby's health.
The pregnancies studied were single babies with no known problems.

stories.headline: A drug found with AI improves breathing in a lung disease trial in China
stories.what_happened: Rentosertib is a drug for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a disease that scars the lungs. The company Insilico Medicine found it using generative AI. In a trial of 71 patients run from Peking Union Medical College Hospital with other Chinese hospitals, people on the highest dose for 12 weeks gained 98 millilitres of breathing capacity on average, while those on a dummy pill lost 20. The trial was published in Nature Medicine.
stories.why_its_good: A medicine that began with an AI system has now been tested against a dummy pill in patients, and the top-dose group's breathing improved while the dummy pill group's got worse.
careful: Small, early trial: 71 patients over 12 weeks, mainly testing safety.
The breathing gain is in the top-dose group of 18 people and needs a larger trial to confirm.
Most patients in every group, including the dummy pill group, reported side effects, and some stopped because of liver problems or diarrhoea.
The drug is not approved anywhere.
Insilico is a company: the independent source is the peer-reviewed paper with hospital investigators.

stories.headline: AI that reads chest X-rays for tuberculosis is now backed by the World Health Organization
stories.what_happened: Since 2021 the World Health Organization has recommended software that reads chest X-rays to screen people aged 15 and over for tuberculosis, and in June 2025 it said six products met its standards. In a study of 23,954 people at three screening centres in Dhaka, Bangladesh, five AI programs were compared with three radiologists, and all five did significantly better. Anyone the software flags still gets a confirming test before treatment.
stories.why_its_good: WHO calls screening with chest X-rays and this software essential for finding tuberculosis cases that are being missed. In the Dhaka study the AI halved the number of confirming tests needed while still catching more than 90% of cases.
careful: The AI screens. It does not diagnose: a positive result needs a confirming test.
WHO does not recommend it for children under 15.
The Dhaka study tested the programs on X-rays taken between 2014 and 2016, not in live use.
The WHO page does not name the countries using it, so do not name any.

stories.headline: An arthritis pill that an AI search flagged for Covid in February 2020 went on to save lives
stories.what_happened: In February 2020 scientists at the London company BenevolentAI, with a doctor from Imperial College London, searched the company's store of medical knowledge, which is built using machine learning, for approved drugs to try against the new coronavirus. They named baricitinib, an arthritis pill, in a letter in The Lancet. In the RECOVERY trial of 8,156 hospital patients, 12% of those given baricitinib died within 28 days against 14% given usual care. In January 2022 the World Health Organization strongly recommended it for severe Covid.
stories.why_its_good: The AI-built search pointed to a pill that was already approved for other uses, in the first weeks of the outbreak, so there was a candidate ready for trials.
careful: The AI produced the suggestion. Large trials run by others proved it.
The letter says the knowledge store uses machine learning: people chose baricitinib from the shortlist it produced.
RECOVERY showed 12% against 14% deaths, a modest gain, and the drug is given alongside steroids.
BenevolentAI is a company: the independent sources are the RECOVERY trial and WHO.
